catalog_quote: The Phonological Word in Wahgi is defined by a unit of stress placement, tone placement, ... and juncture characteristics. ... The subject of Wahgi stress has been the most difficult problem in the phonological analysis of Wahgi. In many words it is indistinguishable from the tonal patterns of those words, however, stress has been analyzed as being phonemic on the basis of its unpredictableness, and is divided into primary stress and secondary stress on the word level. The phonological word carries a unit of primary stress placement, and in words of more than one syllable a possible unit of secondary stress placement. Stress is distinguished by the length and loudness. ... The Wahgi language exhibits at least two degrees of stress, but because of the presence of high tone in most words it is difficult to distinguish whether one is hearing primary stress or high tone in the words in ques…

The held SIL OPD independently says stress is unpredictable/phonemic. (2) Deciding source: Phillips 1976, a Pacific Linguistics phonology-and-morphology monograph (published MA thesis, fieldworker with years of residence, Kuma dialect at Minj = ISO wgi = nucl1620, so no identity problem; the OPD file was borrowed from the North Wahgi folder and is correctly flagged as corroboration only). It is the standard and only modern description; Glottolog and web searches turn up nothing newer on Wahgi [wgi] prosody, and the 2011 SIL tone survey still cites only Phillips and calls the analysis uncertain. sources.quote: 'The analysis of many languages is still uncertain. Just to mention a few, Wahgi (Phillips 1976) is described in terms of word-level melody, and there are only three tone melodies possible per phonological word, but none of the melodies for one-, two- or three-syllable words can be straightforwardly mapped on each other...' No statement on stress placement; secondary survey resting entirely on Phillips 1976.
sources.locator: p.20 (the text layer); bibliography p.22 cites Phillips 1976 only
sources.note: Secondary survey; useful only as a citable statement that the Wahgi word-tone/stress analysis remains uncertain (p.20). Already downloaded.

sources.note: The only other primary phonology of Wahgi (Banz/Middle Wahgi side); Phillips pp.24-25 says Luzbetak treated the unstressed-vowel/stress facts differently ('nonphonemic transitions'), so Luzbetak's own statement on accent placement is the one independent check on Phillips's 'unpredictable, phonemic stress' analysis that our lexical coding rests on.
